analysis.one_liner: Requires owners of aboveground storage tanks to register their tanks, detect and report leaks, carry spill insurance, and pay for cleanups.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: introduced with 16 cosponsors in March 1993, it sat in the House Energy and Commerce Committee, got one subcommittee hearing in September 1994, and died when the 103rd Congress ended in January 1995.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have created the first comprehensive federal program regulating aboveground storage tanks — the large tanks that hold petroleum and other chemicals above ground. Owners would have to tell state authorities where their tanks are, install leak-detection systems, report spills over 42 gallons immediately, upgrade old tanks within 10 years, and show they can pay (roughly $1-2 million in coverage for petroleum tanks) to clean up any release. Tank owners would pay these costs; communities near tanks and people who drink groundwater would get protection from contaminated soil and water.
analysis.who_benefits: People who live near aboveground storage tanks, communities whose drinking water comes from groundwater near tank farms, and state and local emergency responders. The bill requires leak detection, spill reporting, and cleanup (Sec. 5, [S3]), and it makes tank owners — not taxpayers — liable for cleanup costs [S2]. It also applies the rules to federal government tanks, waiving federal immunity so agencies must comply like anyone else (Sec. 9, [S3]).
analysis.who_benefits_short: Communities near fuel and chemical tanks

how_it_helps.text: Requires every owner to notify state or local authorities of each tank's age, size, type, location, and use, and requires states to build full inventories of all tanks holding petroleum or other regulated substances (Sec. 4, [S3]; [S2]).

Directs EPA to issue release detection, prevention, and correction regulations — leak detection systems, inspections, corrosion protection, spill prevention devices, and tank upgrades within 10 years — for every aboveground tank (Sec. 5, [S3]).

Makes tank owners and operators financially liable for cleanup costs and requires them to demonstrate financial responsibility, so taxpayers are not left holding the bill when an operator cannot pay (Sec. 5(c)-(d), 5(i)(6), [S3]; [S2]).

Requires immediate reporting of any petroleum spill of 42 gallons or more and authorizes EPA or the state to take corrective action — including relocating residents and providing alternative drinking water — when an owner is insolvent or cannot be found (Sec. 4(a)(5), 5(i)(5), [S3]).

Subjects federal facilities to the same rules and penalties as private owners, with the United States expressly waiving its immunity, though the President can grant one-year exemptions (Sec. 9, [S3]; [S2]).

analysis.who_pays: Owners and operators of aboveground storage tanks — largely fuel distributors, petroleum and chemical companies, and other businesses that store regulated substances — who bear notification fees, leak-detection and upgrade costs, insurance or bonding costs, and cleanup liability. These costs would ultimately be passed to consumers in fuel and product prices. Taxpayers fund EPA administration and the corrective-action program, though fees collected ($50-$1,000 per tank, scaled to capacity) offset some state inspection costs (Sec. 4(e), Sec. 12, [S3]).
analysis.who_pays_short: Tank owners, fuel distributors, and chemical processors

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs fall on tank owners of all sizes, and the bill acknowledges the impact on small businesses — directing EPA to tailor notice forms and coverage amounts for small business concerns (Sec. 4(c), 5(d)(4)(C), [S3]) — but smaller fuel dealers and farms with larger tanks would still face new detection, upgrade, and insurance expenses that could be passed on to customers.

The bill creates significant new paperwork and administrative burdens: biennial notifications, state inventories, recordkeeping, and a tiered inspection schedule for thousands of facilities (Sec. 4, 5(c)(2), 5(j), [S3]), and authorizes unlimited appropriations for fiscal years 1994-1998 (Sec. 12, [S3]).

The financial responsibility mandate — $1 million to $2 million in coverage per petroleum release — could be hard for some small operators to obtain, which the bill recognizes by letting EPA suspend enforcement where insurance is unavailable and states form risk pools (Sec. 5(d)(4)(D), [S3]).

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is straightforward: prevent and pay for fuel and chemical leaks rather than discover contaminated soil and groundwater after the fact. The bill tries to soften the cost side with small-business carve-outs, scaled fees, exemptions for farm and residential tanks of 1,100 gallons or less, and deferral of insurance requirements until tanks are upgraded. The main honest objection is that the compliance burden lands heavily on smaller operators, and that states and local fire authorities already regulated many of these tanks — the bill lets states run their own approved programs and keeps stricter state rules intact (Sec. 6, [S3]).

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its Transportation and Hazardous Materials Subcommittee, which held a hearing in September 1994, but the committee never voted to send it to the floor before the Congress ended in January 1995.

narrative.text: Rep. James P. Moran (D-VA) introduced the bill on March 16, 1993; it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce [S5].
On March 29, 1993, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Transportation and Hazardous Materials [S5].

The subcommittee held a hearing on September 14, 1994 — the only further action recorded — and the bill was never reported out of committee or voted on by either chamber before the 103rd Congress ended on January 3, 1995 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Tank owners and operators — especially petroleum and chemical storage businesses — were better off, avoiding notification fees, leak-detection and upgrade costs, and $1-2 million insurance requirements. Communities near unregulated tanks continued to bear the risk of undetected spills and groundwater contamination.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Tank owners and fuel storage operators

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship was nearly all Democratic — 15 of 16 cosponsors were Democrats, with one Republican (Rep. Wolf) — and the bill never reached a floor vote where party lines could be tested.

industries.industry: Petroleum storage and distribution (tank owners and operators)
industries.note: Owners would pay notification fees, install leak detection, upgrade aging tanks within 10 years, and carry $1-2 million in coverage per release — real compliance costs passed partly to consumers. Their interest in avoiding those costs runs against the public's interest in early leak detection and funded cleanups.

industries.industry: Chemical manufacturers and processors storing regulated substances
industries.note: The same registration, inspection, financial responsibility, and corrective-action requirements apply to tanks holding CERCLA regulated substances (non-hazardous-waste), adding cost and liability for chemical handlers.
The bill creates a new mandated market: tank owners must show financial responsibility through insurance, surety bonds, letters of credit, or state funds, generating demand for coverage products.

industries.industry: Small fuel dealers and farms with small tanks
industries.note: Farm and residential tanks of 1,100 gallons or less, small heating-oil tanks, and small fire-protected tanks under local fire codes are excluded or lightly treated, and fees scale down to $50 for small facilities — shielding most small household-scale operators.
